paragraphs: This occupation corresponds to U.S. O*NET/BLS 25-1051.00, teaching physical science courses other than chemistry and physics, including atmospheric, earth, marine, and space sciences. The scope includes both teaching-focused and teaching-and-research teachers; the 26 tasks cover lesson preparation, lecturing, discussion, grading, student supervision, laboratory and field teaching, independent research, publication, grant applications, and departmental service, and not every position carries out all of them. Mainland China's occupational classification can only serve as a broad category reference and is not a one-to-one correspondence with the detailed U.S. occupation; teaching in higher education institutions requires verifying teacher qualification and appointment requirements. Article Forty-Six of the Higher Education Law of Mainland China provides that a person with a graduate or undergraduate degree, with the corresponding teaching ability and having passed the qualification assessment, may obtain a higher education institution teacher qualification; those without such a degree but with substantial learning also have a statutory path through the national teacher qualification examination and assessment. Those holding a doctorate or being considered for appointment as associate professor or above apply the simplified assessment conditions under Article Nine of the Implementation Measures for the Regulations on Teacher Qualifications, but assessment is still required. Recommendation by two professors or associate professors is an examination application condition under Article Eleven of the Regulations on Teacher Qualifications, not a uniform requirement for all assessment applications.

Three short self-test tasks: write the syllabus points for one 90-minute undergraduate course (learning objectives, reading materials, classroom activities, assessment methods, and time allocation); use fictional data to complete grading and feedback for an observation record or course assignment (grading rubric, comments, and improvement suggestions); and write a two-page statement for a funder about a planned study (research question, existing data gaps, methods, expected contribution, and data and safety considerations). (Editorial suggestion, not hiring, promotion review, or a teaching ability test, nor a statement about any institution's procedures.)

People who are more likely to adapt: willing to lecture and demonstrate to students long term and to accept public expression and being evaluated, able to arrange time among teaching, research, and practice (76% of respondents work more than 40 hours per week and 12% work 40 hours), able to continuously produce reviewable data or research results and to withstand competitive situations (18% consider it highly competitive and 54% moderately competitive; publication and funding competition are not listed separately), and willing to supervise students and practice according to academic standards and ethical requirements. If you are unwilling to lecture publicly long term and accept student and peer evaluation, find it hard to keep advancing research while arranging your own time, are unwilling to record grades and supervision processes according to standards, or are not psychologically prepared for competition over results and funding, the risk is usually greater.

U.S. occupation-specific definition: the 2025 median wage is 103,170 USD; the 10/25/75/90 percentiles are 59,700/77,260/135,510/203,190 USD, with no hourly wage provided. BLS current projection: about 12,000 in 2025, growth of 2.4% over 2025—2035, about 12,300 in 2035, an official net increase of about 300, and about 800 job openings per year. The higher education teacher group listed in the OOH is 1,378,200 in 2025, growth of 7% over 2025—2035, a net increase of 98,200, and 103,300 openings per year, and cannot be treated as this occupation's standalone figure. Mainland China wages provide only industry and position category references; qualifications and appointment are verified against Chinese regulations and position announcements.

One line: teach atmospheric, earth, marine, or space science at a college or university and take on courses and student supervision; some positions also carry out research and publication in the field.

The work of postsecondary atmospheric, earth, marine, and space sciences teachers can be divided into four categories: teaching and course development (preparing lecture notes and course materials, teaching atmospheric, earth, marine, and space science courses to undergraduates and graduate students, leading classroom discussion, grading assignments and theses, planning, evaluating, and revising course content and teaching methods, and compiling topical bibliographies); supervising students (keeping regular office hours to tutor students, supervising degree theses and observation and experiments, supervising undergraduate and graduate teaching and research work, writing recommendation letters, and serving as an adviser to student organizations); research and scholarly output (conducting observation and data research in the field, publishing results in professional journals, monographs, or academic conferences, writing grant applications and reviewing others' applications, reviewing for professional journals, and collaborating with colleagues to solve teaching and research problems); and administration and professional service (participating in departmental and university committees and institutional matters, taking on administrative duties such as department chair, participating in student recruitment, registration, and job placement, participating in campus and community activities, providing professional consulting to government or industry, and attending academic conferences to stay current in the field).

O*NET 25-1051.00: teaches physical science courses other than chemistry and physics, including those whose main role is teaching and those who combine teaching and research. Respondent position examples include atmospheric science professor, astronomy professor, geology professor, oceanography professor, meteorology professor, earth science professor, lecturer, and professor. Interest code SI (Social, Investigative); the 26 tasks describe group duties. Job Zone Five and SVP 8.0 or above indicate a need for extensive preparation; 46% of respondents believe a master's is required, 29% a doctorate, and 16% postdoctoral training, which is not the hiring probability for each degree.

Assessment and feedback | Grade according to standards and give improvement suggestions | Write, administer, and grade examinations, review and grade assignments and theses, follow grading standards, and state the basis and directions for improvement in the comments.

Supervising students | Bring students to the point of doing observation and research independently | Keep regular office hours to tutor students, supervise degree theses and observation and experiments, supervise students' laboratory and field teaching practice, provide advice on students' academic and career development, and write recommendation letters.

Research and publication | Continuously produce reviewable results | Conduct observation and data research in the field, publish results in professional journals, monographs, or academic conferences, and review for professional journals.

Funding and collaboration | Make research sustainable | Write grant applications to obtain external research funding and review others' applications, collaborate with colleagues to solve teaching and research problems, and attend academic conferences to stay current in the field.

Administration and professional service | Support the operation of the department and discipline | Participate in academic and administrative committees handling institutional, departmental, and academic matters, take on administrative duties such as department chair, participate in student recruitment, registration, job placement, and campus and community activities, and provide professional consulting to government or industry.

The weight of the four task categories differs across institution types (research universities, teaching-focused institutions, and community colleges): research universities emphasize research output and graduate supervision more, teaching-focused institutions emphasize teaching load and undergraduate teaching more, and community colleges focus on teaching and usually do not require research output; the same title may involve very different actual requirements at different institutions.

Define course objectives: state the learning objectives and assessment methods. → Prepare materials: write the syllabus, lecture notes, and observation and experiment plans. → Deliver teaching: lecture and demonstrate methods and lead discussion and experiments. → Assess and give feedback: grade according to standards and give improvement suggestions. → Supervise students: answer questions and supervise degree theses and observation and experiments. → Advance research and publication: publish results, apply for funding, and revise courses.

Teaching records (syllabi, grades and attendance, comments and feedback, supervision records) and research records (observation data, experiment and analysis records, manuscripts and review comments) are the basic materials that make the teaching and scholarly process reviewable and traceable; when student grades and identity information, unpublished data, or observation records are involved, they must be retained and handled according to institutional and ethics committee requirements and must not be disclosed freely; citing others' data and materials requires noting the source.

BLS Table1.2 lists 25-1051 separately: about 12,000 in 2025, growth of 2.4% over 2025—2035, about 12,300 in 2035, an official net increase of about 300, and about 800 job openings per year. Job openings include net growth and demand from leaving the labor force and occupational transfers, and cannot be treated as net growth or an individual's employment probability. Lesson preparation: state the learning objectives and the reading and activity arrangements. → Teaching: lecture and lead discussion and questions. → Office hours: tutor students at fixed times and keep records. → Grading: grade according to the rubric and write comments and improvement suggestions. → Supervision: supervise student theses and laboratory and field teaching practice. → Debrief: revise the course according to student feedback and research progress.

Article Forty-Six of Mainland China's Higher Education Law sets out teacher qualification for Chinese citizens: a person with a graduate or undergraduate degree, with the corresponding teaching ability and having passed the qualification assessment, may obtain a higher education institution teacher qualification; those without such a degree but with substantial learning also have a statutory path through the national teacher qualification examination and assessment. Those holding a doctorate or being considered for appointment as associate professor or above apply the simplified assessment conditions under Article Nine of the Implementation Measures for the Regulations on Teacher Qualifications, but assessment is still required. Recommendation by two professors or associate professors is an examination application condition under Article Eleven of the Regulations on Teacher Qualifications, not a uniform requirement for all assessment applications. Article Thirteen of the Regulations on Teacher Qualifications provides for the authority for assessment, with entrusted institutions assessing the qualifications of their own serving or prospective appointees; Article Forty-Seven of the Higher Education Law lists the positions of teaching assistant, lecturer, associate professor, and professor, and Article Forty-Eight implements an appointment system. Specific materials and timing are verified against the local assessment announcement.
Retain the original values and correction records, and mark simulated materials as fictional.

Look at four things for boundaries: who is responsible for teaching and assessment, who is responsible for research judgments and data conclusions, who is responsible for institutional administration and policy decisions, and who is responsible for students' degree conferral and academic status management. Postsecondary atmospheric, earth, marine, and space sciences teachers design courses and deliver teaching and assessment within their duties, carry out research and publish results, supervise students, and give academic advice; degree conferral, academic status management, and credit recognition are decided by the institution according to its rules; teacher appointment and promotion review are carried out by the institution and the review bodies according to the rules; field observation and laboratory work must be carried out according to procedures under conditions that meet safety and permit requirements. Teaching content and research conclusions cannot replace the institution's administrative decisions or legal judgments, and matters involving academic misconduct, ethical disputes, or students' major interests must be reported through institutional procedures.
Within the scope of duties, complete course design, teaching and assessment, student supervision, and research output, and deliver reviewable teaching and scholarly records.

Answer teaching and scholarly delivery questions with "what are the teaching objectives and assessment standards, have students met the learning objectives, are the data process and conclusion statements reviewable, and are academic standards and ethical requirements met".

Independent research, publication, and professional consulting for government or industry can be part of this occupation's tasks; positions that only do observation, pure research, or administration without higher education teaching duties should be classified separately according to the actual tasks. Final policy decisions on degree conferral, academic status management, and teacher appointment are not replaced by individual teachers.

The objects are undergraduates' and graduate students' learning and disciplinary knowledge, and one's own research questions; the basis is disciplinary theory, methods, and pedagogy, the institution's course and assessment systems and academic standards, research ethics and student information protection requirements, and provisions such as the Higher Education Law of the People's Republic of China.

Postsecondary atmospheric, earth, marine, and space sciences teachers teach physical science courses other than chemistry and physics in higher education (including meteorology and atmospheric science, geology and earth science, oceanography, and space science) and combine teaching with research practice: preparing lecture notes and course materials, organizing classroom discussion and laboratory and field teaching, evaluating and grading assignments and theses, supervising student degree theses and observation and experiments, conducting observation and data research in the field, publishing results and applying for funding, and taking on student supervision and academic and administrative service. China's higher education teacher classification serves only as a broad category reference, and the formal detailed code's mapping to the U.S. detailed occupation was not confirmed this round; teaching in higher education institutions requires obtaining a higher education institution teacher qualification under the Higher Education Law of the People's Republic of China and the Regulations on Teacher Qualifications; the U.S. wage and employment figures are the occupation-specific definitions shown by O*NET (2025 median annual wage 103,170 USD, about 12,000 in 2025, growth of 2.4% over 2025—2035 with about 800 openings per year), and the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook's "Postsecondary Teachers" group definition (about 1,378,200 jobs in 2025, growth of 7% over 2025—2035) is labeled separately.

Learning management systems and online teaching tools, reference management and statistical analysis software, numerical computing and visualization software, and geographic information systems and remote sensing data processing tools can be used for course delivery, material organization, and research analysis, but setting learning objectives, assessment standards and grading judgments, research questions and conclusions, and academic standards judgments remain the teacher's responsibility and must be recorded truthfully, and tool outputs cannot replace teaching and scholarly judgment.
Define course objectives → prepare materials → deliver teaching → assess and give feedback → supervise students → advance research and revise the course.

Measure by whether the learning objectives are met, whether grading and feedback follow standards and have a basis, whether the data process and conclusion statements are reviewable, whether academic standards and ethical requirements are met, and whether student supervision records are complete, not by a single teaching evaluation score or a single paper.

Syllabi and lecture notes and assignments, examination papers and grading rubrics and comments, student supervision and office hour records, recommendation letters and supervision records, observation data and experiment and analysis records, papers and conference reports and review records, grant applications and project completion materials, and course evaluation and improvement records.

Divide responsibilities according to teaching and research duties and institutional systems; before starting, verify the position's teaching workload and research assessment requirements, appointment and promotion conditions, safety and ethics requirements for supervising students and field and laboratory teaching, rules for managing student personal information and unpublished data, and compliance requirements for the use of funds and outside consulting.

Course design, teaching, and assessment are the teacher's responsibility; research judgments and responsibility for results rest with the researcher; degree conferral, academic status, and credit recognition are decided by the institution according to the rules; teacher appointment and promotion review are the responsibility of the institution and the review bodies; field observation and laboratory work must implement safety review and data permits according to institutional and regulatory authority rules.

In Mainland China, first verify the target discipline, degree, and teaching and research conditions, then apply for the applicable higher education institution teacher qualification assessment; statutory qualification conditions and employer appointment conditions are different. Nanjing University's 2026 tenure-track positions in directions such as marine geoscience require a relevant doctorate and teaching and research ability, which is a single-institution sample. The U.S. O*NET education survey gives 46% master's, 29% doctorate, and 16% postdoctoral training; BLS typical entry-level education separately lists a doctorate or professional degree, using a different statistical method.

Teaching and research must follow academic standards and ethical requirements: student personal information and unpublished data require processing authorization under the applicable rules; whether a project needs ethics review is determined by the research content and institutional systems; citing others' data and materials requires noting the source, and data or scores must not be fabricated or falsified; student personal information and unpublished data must be kept confidential as required; academic misconduct and conflicts of interest must be declared and handled through institutional procedures.

When a grading record is found inconsistent with the original materials, a data or observation process's source cannot be verified, ethical disputes or conflicts of interest are involved, or a student raises a major objection about grades or supervision, the relevant processing should be paused, the original records retained, and review and reporting carried out through institutional procedures, and records or conclusions must not be modified because of teaching progress or assessment pressure.

Teaching effects and research conclusions apply only to specific course conditions, student groups, data, and methods; the same teaching method or hypothesis may perform differently at different institutions and on different datasets, and a single teaching evaluation result must not be presented as a general conclusion, nor may preliminary research results be presented as confirmed disciplinary findings.

Work patterns (76% of respondents work more than 40 hours per week and 12% work 40 hours; 33% sit more than half the time, and the work includes public lecturing (49% daily)): teaching, research, and administrative service coexist, and whether field observation and laboratory duty are included depends on the course and project arrangements.
Look at the position type and assessment requirements, not the position title.

Position types: research universities (mainly research and graduate supervision), teaching-focused institutions (mainly undergraduate teaching), community colleges (mainly teaching, usually without a research output requirement), and part-time or lecturer positions (appointed by course); the workload, assessment, and stability differ greatly across types.
Degree and qualification requirements determine whether you can apply and be appointed.

Degree and qualifications: verify the position's degree, discipline, and teaching or publication experience requirements, and the applicable conditions and submission timing for higher education institution teacher qualification assessment in Mainland China; simplified conditions such as those for a doctorate do not mean the qualification is obtained automatically.
The assessment and promotion system directly determines work intensity and career stability.

Assessment and promotion: the assessment standards for the appointment period (teaching load, teaching evaluations, papers, and projects), whether an up-or-out arrangement exists, the conditions for promotion review and position advancement, and the renewal rules for part-time and lecturer positions.
The time allocation between teaching and research and the competitive pressure affect long-term sustainability.

Work patterns: 76% of respondents work more than 40 hours per week and 12% work 40 hours, and teaching, research, and administrative service coexist; 18% consider it highly competitive and 54% moderately competitive, and competition over publication and funding directly affects assessment results, which must be verified against the actual contract and assessment rules.
Degree level, publication record, and project experience determine long-term development and income level.

Development pathways: whether you can complete a doctorate and postdoctoral training, publish continuously and lead projects, pass the appointment-period assessment and promotion review, or move into teaching-focused institutions, research institutions, meteorological, marine, and geological observation agencies, and environmental and climate policy and consulting directions.
First verify official and institutional requirements, then decide how much to invest.

Use institutional public recruitment and promotion review documents and the education administration's rules on teacher qualification assessment as the standard, verify whether the degree, qualifications, and teaching experience pathways are compliant, and do not trust non-official agencies' promises of guaranteed admission, guaranteed appointment to an authorised staff position, or guaranteed promotion.

paragraphs: Suggested order of choice: first settle the position direction (a teaching-and-research position at a research university, a teaching position at a teaching-focused institution or community college, or a practical training position oriented toward observation and experimental practice teaching), then look at the discipline direction (atmospheric and meteorological, geological and earth, marine, space science) and the evidence you can present. Adjacent directions (postsecondary physics teachers, postsecondary chemistry teachers, postsecondary environmental science teachers, postsecondary geography teachers, natural sciences managers, postsecondary teachers) have similar daily task structures, but the disciplinary objects, assessment standards, and qualification requirements differ, so they cannot be swapped based only on the job title.

Oriented toward environmental systems and cross-disciplinary scientific questions; materials are mainly environmental monitoring data and models; compared with this occupation the disciplinary boundary leans more toward environmental processes and the policy interface, and the course and assessment structure is similar but the disciplinary object differs.
People who would rather approach physical science through environmental monitoring and environmental process research.
Teaching environmental science courses, conducting environmental monitoring and simulation research, and supervising degree theses.

Oriented toward chemical substances and reactions; O*NET 25-1051.00 explicitly excludes chemistry courses from this occupation. Compared with this occupation the experimental objects and methodological systems differ, and the teaching responsibility structure is similar but the disciplinary object differs.
People who would rather do chemical experiments and substance research.
Teaching chemistry courses, conducting chemical experiment research, and supervising degree theses.

Teaches physics courses, and the objects of study may cover theory, experiment, and observation. The key difference from this occupation is the disciplinary course definition; O*NET lists physics teachers 25-1054 and this occupation 25-1051 separately.

Teaching physics courses, conducting physics experiments and theoretical research, and supervising degree theses.

Materials and conditions

All are fictional exercises. Minghu University plans to offer a 16-week undergraduate course, 90 minutes per week, with 60 students, of which 20 are non-majors; no real field sampling is required. Training objectives: distinguish surface temperature from air temperature, align spatial and temporal scales, and explain data limitations. The grading prompt is five fictional short reports, each worth 10 points: A cites Figure 1 without a source; B writes an air temperature of 30℃ without time or station; C directly subtracts a nighttime 2-meter air temperature of 25℃ from a midday satellite surface temperature of 35℃ and calls the result a 10℃ heat island; D fills missing satellite pixels with 0℃ and then averages; E claims a year-round effect from a single clear-day observation and lists no limitations. Any parts not described are treated as meeting the requirements.

Grading rubric: sources and traceability 2 points, measurement definition and same-scale comparison 3 points, missing-data handling 2 points, conclusions and limitations 3 points. For each report, deduct only the full value of the item corresponding to the described defect and give full marks on the other items; suspected misconduct is only checked through the process and is not directly penalized through the exercise.

Research concept: use public or fictional paired urban and suburban data to compare the same-day, same-time surface temperature difference with the 2-meter air temperature difference; this exercise provides no measured values and does not calculate a real effect. The funder requires a two-page statement stating the variables, pairing method, missing-data rules, contribution, and limitations.
Exercise tasks

Task one: write a 16-week course syllabus listing three checkable objectives, the weekly arrangement, material sources, and assessment weights; also write the timetable for one 90-minute class, whose total time must equal 90. Task two: calculate the A—E scores using the given 10-point rubric, write one sentence on the basis for each problem and one actionable revision, and explain how to self-check before course submission to prevent errors.

Task three: write a two-page research statement: research question and variables, existing data gaps, methods, expected contribution, data permissions, and safety boundaries; when there is no data, keep the plan and do not fill in fictional measured results.
Reference deliverable

Course example: weeks 1—2 introduction and measurement definitions, weeks 3—4 radiation and scale, weeks 5—6 ground records, weeks 7—8 satellite data, weeks 9—10 pairing and missing data, weeks 11—12 uncertainty, weeks 13—14 group analysis, weeks 15—16 presentation and debrief. Objectives are verified separately by concept discrimination, pairing design, and limitation statements; assignments 30%, group report 30%, final project 40%, totaling 100%. 90-minute class example: introduction 10, measurement definition lecture 20, fictional data pairing exercise 25, group error diagnosis 20, reporting and quiz 10, summary 5, totaling 90 minutes; do not mistake the 16-week syllabus for a single class.

Grading answers: A=8 (2 points deducted for sources), add the source and data date for Figure 1; B=7 (3 points deducted for definition and scale), add the station, time, and measurement height; C=7 (3 points deducted for the same item), compare the same-scale, same-time urban-suburban differences separately and do not mix surface temperature with air temperature as one indicator; D=8 (2 points deducted for missing data), keep the missing-data flag and disclose the number of valid samples; E=7 (3 points deducted for conclusions and limitations), limit the conclusion to that clear day and state the seasonal and weather limitations.

Two-page statement reference: the first page presents the urban-suburban pairing question, the selection rules for the same day, same time, and same measurement definition, and the data still missing; the second page calculates the two types of temperature difference separately, discloses missing data and uncertainty, and plans to extend the seasonal sample; write only the expected contribution and do not claim to have proven a year-round urban heat island. entries.answer: The daily work revolves around four task categories: teaching and course development (preparing lecture notes and course materials, teaching atmospheric, earth, marine, and space science courses to undergraduates and graduate students, organizing classroom discussion and laboratory and field teaching, planning, evaluating, and revising course content and teaching methods, and compiling topical bibliographies); assessment and feedback (writing, administering, and grading examinations, reviewing and grading assignments and theses, and giving actionable feedback according to standards); student supervision and research (keeping regular office hours to tutor students, supervising degree theses and observation and experiments, conducting observation and data research in the field, publishing results in professional journals and academic conferences, and writing grant applications and reviewing others' applications); and academic and administrative service (participating in departmental and university committees and institutional matters, taking on administrative duties such as department chair, participating in student recruitment and career guidance, and providing professional consulting to government or industry). O*NET 25-1051.00 lists 26 tasks covering the above scope; research universities, teaching-focused institutions, and community colleges differ greatly in the weight of the four task categories.

subject.name: Postsecondary atmospheric, earth, marine, and space sciences teachers
subject.summary: This occupation corresponds to U.S. O*NET25-1051.00 and involves teaching physical science courses other than chemistry and physics at colleges and universities, including atmospheric, earth, marine, and space sciences. It includes both those whose main role is teaching and those who combine teaching and research. Duties cover course design, lecturing, grading, student supervision, and laboratory and field teaching; some positions carry out independent research, publication, and departmental service. U.S. Job Zone Five indicates a need for extensive preparation; teacher qualifications and appointment in Mainland China require separate verification under local regulations and institutional requirements, and broad category references cannot be treated as a one-to-one correspondence with the detailed U.S. occupation.
